start.text: Constable Rell is standing where he has evidently been standing for some hours. 'You'd be the widow's man. Look all you like. It's apoplexy, and looking won't make it anything else.'

choices.text: Did anyone hear anything the night before?
I'd like the keys to the strongbox.

morning.text:
'Half six. Shutters still up, door fast, and Mrs. Ackroyd across the way saying he'd not opened, which he has done every morning for thirty-one years.'

'I put my shoulder to it and the frame came away. And then half the Row came in behind me, which I'd have stopped if I'd had four more hands.'

night.text: 'The house opposite. Heard his shop bell at the ninth bell of St. Ferrin, and a voice raised after it.' He shrugs. 'One voice. Or two, they said, when I pressed. People hear what fits by morning.'

keys_ask.text:
'The ring stays with me. It's constabulary property until the estate's settled.'

He says it the way a man says a thing he has said before and would very much like to be talked out of.

choices.text: Offer him something for his trouble.
Suggest, gently, that he wants to hand them over.

keys_paid.text: The coins go into his glove without either of you looking at them. 'Back by dark,' he says. 'And you didn't have them.'

keys_pressed.text: He hands them over before he has finished deciding to, and then stands there with the shape of a refusal still on his face. 'Back by dark,' he says, uncertainly.

start.text: Ilsabet Crane has not sat down since you arrived. 'They wrote apoplexy on the fourteenth of a week he spent nailing his own shutters shut. I am not clever, but I can put those two beside each other.'

choices.text: Tell me about the last week.
What did he take in that he shouldn't have?

week.text:
'He slept here. In the shop, on a chair, with the poker across his knees. He would not say what for.'

She presses the back of her wrist to her mouth for a moment and takes it away again.

'The last thing he asked me — and he asked it twice — was whether a thing can be given back to a man who never comes for it.'

pledge.text: 'I don't know his stock. He kept the book for that.' She glances at the counter and away. 'He was a careful man, and careful men do not start sleeping with a poker over nothing.'

cass.text:
'Cass?' Something crosses her face and she puts it away. 'Ezra thought the world of him. Said he had a head for figures.'

'He's been here since six this morning, crying on and off. Grief looks like that sometimes. It looks like other things too.'

start.text:
Cass Whitlow is nineteen and has been awake for a day and a half. His hands do not stop moving. 'You're the one she hired. I've already told the constable everything, I don't know what else I'm —'

He stops, and starts again more carefully. 'Ask what you like.'

choices.text: The last ferry across the Ash is at seven.
Whose hand wrote the last eleven days of the ledger?
Read what he is not saying.

alibi.text:
'Locked up at eight. Crossed the Ash, walked out to my mother's at Barrow Fields, slept there. Heard at noon from a boy in the lane.'

He says it in one breath, in exactly the order he said it to the constable.

broken.text:
You put the ferryman's hours to him, plainly, and watch him arrive at the end of the sentence a long way behind you.

He does not say anything. He does not say anything for so long that the not-saying becomes the answer, and both of you hear it happen.

ledger.text:
'He'd been letting me make the entries. His eyes.' His voice goes up half a step. 'His eyes were going, everyone knew that, ask anybody —'

Nobody has said anything about the old man's eyes all day.

read.text:
You say the one thing he has spent all night preparing not to be asked, and it lands somewhere behind his sternum.

'I didn't — ' he says. 'I only meant to take the — ' and then he shuts his mouth so hard you hear his teeth.

bye.text: He nods too many times and goes back to not sleeping.

start.text: Sil Mowbray is coiling a wet rope badly and in no hurry. 'Ferry's done for the day. Ferry's done for the day about four hours before people think it is, which is most of my conversation.'

choices.text: When is the last crossing to Barrow Fields?
Who's been buying odd things off the Row?

ferry.text:
The coins vanish somewhere into the rope coil.

'Seven o'clock, and that's the summer table. No bridge for four mile either way. Anybody tells you they crossed the Ash after seven, they walked on it.'

vane.text:
'Gentleman name of Vane. Three months now. Buys clockwork — queer clockwork, watches that don't tell time, that sort. Pays over the odds and doesn't haggle, which round here is the same as shouting.'

'Halloway's boy took the ferry out to him twice that I saw. Carrying, both times.'

halloway.text: 'Bought my father's tools off us in a bad year and sold them back at what he paid. Not many would.' He spits into the water. 'Whatever finished him, it wasn't owed.'

bye.text: He goes back to ruining the rope.
